attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: Dropping 'magically' slightly changes the tone, but the contract reads the claim as 'substantial maintenance difficulties remain', which keeps the original scope. It is a present-tense observation about current tools.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary and does not deny that AI helps. Using early 2025 as the window for 'current' tools is a reasonable choice by the evaluator. The contract also requires evidence of upkeep over time, which fits the words 'over time'.

evidence.note: A real preprint on fixing maintainability issues. It found that most fixes introduced errors or new issues. Its replication package dates the experiments to 2024, so under the source rule it is earlier-period context. It also tests single fixes, not ongoing upkeep.

reviews.rationale: The only item is an earlier-period study of one-off repairs. It points toward continued limitations but does not meet the contract's requirement for target-period, longitudinal maintenance evidence. Nothing in the packet shows tools reliably handling sustained maintenance either. The evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post.

semantics.note: 'Will lead' is an unhedged prediction of an existential outcome ('in some instances') with no deadline. The content is causal, but the claim is a forecast. The contract's forecast_outcome axis fits this. The qualifiers are preserved.

contract.note: Reading 'overdependence' as uncritical acceptance of generated code is fair, and so is requiring both the maintenance and security consequences. The early-resolution rule is appropriately strict.

evidence.note: A Fall 2025 novice study showing generated code accepted with little review. This establishes the antecedent only. It does not show large accumulations of spaghetti code or security consequences, so it is not evidence of the outcome.
Veracode's security testing of generated code. It is not tied to beginners or to overdependence, so it is context only.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline. The early-resolution rule needs dated evidence of beginner overdependence causing both hard-to-maintain code and security problems. The packet shows overdependence and general security risk, but not the full causal chain. Nothing contradicts the forecast. It stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post.

semantics.note: An accurate restatement of a present-tense claim covering all three named areas.

contract.note: The plain reading (human expertise is still materially needed) is ordinary, and the early-2025 window is a reasonable choice for 'current'. The contract correctly separates implementing stated requirements from discovering what clients want.

evidence.note: SWE-Lancer, published Feb 2025: frontier models could not solve most real bug-fix and implementation-decision tasks. This supports the debugging part and partly the technical-decision part. It does not test client requirements.
Anthropic's announcement of its own model, Feb 2025. As a company disclosure, it describes strong coding results but does not show human expertise becoming unnecessary.

reviews.rationale: The support condition needs established dependence on human expertise in all three areas. E1 supports the debugging part and partly the technical-decision part. No evidence addresses architecture design as a whole or discovering client needs, and nothing contradicts any part. Taken together, the evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post.

semantics.note: Calling the idea 'absurd' is a firm statement that coders and architects are not heading toward obsolescence because of AI. It is reasonably treated as an open-ended negative forecast. 'Due to AI' matches the context.

contract.note: Reading the claim as rejecting AI-driven obsolescence, rather than promising unchanged employment, is fair. The contract correctly declines to bring in the separate 'next year' remark as a deadline.

evidence.note: A Stanford payroll study showing a decline for young developers while older age groups grew. It does not establish obsolescence or show that AI caused the change, so it is context only.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated, and the packet contains no conclusive dated event showing broad, lasting AI-driven obsolescence. Pressure on early-career employment does not meet the contradiction condition. Continued employment at one point in time cannot confirm an open-ended forecast, so the claim stays unresolved.
